demographics.trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one

vignette:
Rosa's Story

Rosa has worked the second shift at the automotive parts factory for twelve years. She knows every station on the line, every supervisor, every shortcut through the warehouse. The work is repetitive and physically demanding, but it's honest work that has allowed her to support herself and help her younger brother with his college tuition. She takes pride in her consistency-she's rarely missed a day.

Three months ago, everything fractured.

Her mother, Elena, was 67 and had always been the center of Rosa's world. They lived ten minutes apart, spoke almost daily, and Rosa visited every Sunday with groceries and homemade food. Elena had minor health issues-some arthritis, slightly elevated blood pressure-nothing that seemed serious. When Rosa called her mother on a Tuesday evening after her shift, Elena sounded tired but normal. They made plans for the weekend.

The next morning, Rosa's brother called. Their mother had collapsed in the kitchen. By the time the ambulance arrived, it was too late. A massive stroke. The doctors said it would have been instantaneous, that she wouldn't have suffered. Rosa isn't sure if that's supposed to comfort her.

Since then, everything has changed.

The factory floor, once familiar, now feels suffocating. Rosa still goes to work-she can't afford not to-but the fluorescent lights make her head pound, and the repetitive mechanical sounds trigger a panic that rises from her chest without warning. Last week, a machine backfired loudly, and Rosa found herself on the ground without remembering how she got there, her coworkers standing over her with concerned faces. She told them she'd tripped, but she knows they didn't believe her.

At night, Rosa lies awake replaying that Tuesday phone call. She torments herself with questions: What if she'd driven over that evening? What if she'd insisted her mother see a cardiologist? The "what ifs" spiral endlessly, stealing her sleep. When she does drift off, she dreams of finding her mother on the kitchen floor, but in the dreams it's always different-sometimes Rosa is frozen and can't call for help; sometimes her mother's eyes are open and accusing.

The apartment feels cavernous now. Rosa has stopped cooking elaborate meals. She eats cereal standing at the sink, unable to sit at the table where her mother used to sit. Her brother calls regularly, but she finds it hard to talk. He seems to be moving forward-he attended a grief support group, he's returned to his routines-and Rosa feels ashamed of her inability to do the same. She's irritable with him in ways she doesn't intend, snapping at him for small things, then feeling guilty for hours.

What troubles Rosa most is the intrusive guilt. She replays moments from years past: times she was impatient with her mother, times she cancelled plans, times she was too tired to listen fully to her stories. These memories ambush her at unexpected moments-while folding laundry, while driving, while standing at her station at work. The guilt is physical, a weight pressing against her ribs.

She's started avoiding things. She hasn't returned to the church where her mother was a regular. She's declined invitations from friends. She keeps her phone on silent because she can't bear to hear others' voices or their attempts at sympathy. Even the grocery store feels dangerous-she might see someone who knew her mother, or worse, she might turn a corner and forget for a moment that her mother is gone, then remember all over again.

Rosa doesn't think of herself as someone who struggles with her mental health. She's always been the strong one, the reliable one. But three months after losing her mother, she recognizes that something fundamental has shifted, and she doesn't know how to find her way back.
